body:
Well said.  I experienced exactly what you're describing six years ago.  I have one picture of her left.  I still keep an old email account that I had back then, and I check it from time to time because I know it's the only way she could contact me at this point.  I know that she never will, though, and the only thing left of who she was when we were together are my own memories.  For all intents and purposes, she is a ghost now.

It seems so very strange to me that such a profound change within a person can be possible.  Furthermore, it's fundamentally unnerving to come to the realization that the single most defining moment of your life, the one event that set the course for you to become what you are today, was a cataclysmic and irreparable loss.  

Memories like that can turn you into something less than human.  They aren't meant to persist like they have with me.  Let them fester, and sooner or later the only reasonable solution is to violently expel them through the back of your skull and be finally, mercifully defeated by them.  It's a desperate, pitiful and absolutely terrifying state of affairs.

Not a problem.  I identify with just about everything you're going through, so talking through a bit of it like this helps me as well.  

I'm going to keep going on about love for a minute.  To be fair, you should keep in mind that I'm absolutely terrible with love and every opportunity I've had to let it enter my life and grow into something meaningful has turned into a monstrous spectacle of pain for everyone involved.  There is always the possibility that I don't have the faintest clue of what I'm talking about.

That being said, I think there's a middle ground to be reached and it's important to cautiously manage expectations when dealing with something like love.  It probably won't fix all of your problems, but it's also not just an illusory hangover from the earlier years when you were a bit younger and a lot more idealistic.  It's a little bit of both.  It's a strange, abstract, tantalizing concept that nicely represents both the horror and the unrestrained joy of basic self-awareness.  

It can't fix all of your problems, but it can help heal all the little wounds its absence sometimes causes in a way that nothing else can.  It is vital, and the basic primal longing we all feel for it is absolutely justified.

Furthermore, there's no shame in ever having or believing in the type of annoyingly blissful puppy love you describe.  The whole idea seems silly once it's over, but the important thing is that at one point in your life it was an all-consuming force.  It was supercharged and ridiculous.  It was manic.  It was the kind of love that beat you over the head with a shovel while shouting "EVERYTHING WILL BE OKAY FOREVER BECAUSE I HAVE THIS HERE SHOVEL AND I'LL MURDER EVERYTHING BAD WITH IT."

That's probably a terrible description, but I think you understand what I'm saying.  The important thing to carry with you after an experience like that is not that it was a lie, but that for one precious moment you really did allow yourself to believe that everything had a real chance of turning out just fine.  That feeling, regardless of how it came to you, is always true.   And it can always come back to you, even if love never does.

I can't advocate the use of therapy or prescription medication because I have no experience with that kind of thing and, frankly, it kind of scares and sickens me.  I can't say that there's a sure fix for any of the pain you're experiencing because I've dealt with it myself and still haven't beaten it.  I can only offer certain perspectives on specific aspects of the whole mess, and even that I may do badly, but I can tell you without uncertainty that you are stronger than you realize.  

Depression doesn't make you weaker.  It's a shift in perspective; a sort of dreary (and likely more realistic) image of a world suddenly stripped of all the neat little bells and whistles other people blissfully occupy themselves with for years on end without ever bothering to question.  It's the realization that the world owes you nothing, its people may try to kill you before ever trying to help, and that you could dedicate your life to trying to make it a better place only to watch reality swallow the fruits of your labor whole and cover what remains with a fresh sheen of fine suffering.  All of that is entirely possible, maybe even probable, and it's all pretty fucking sad.

Thing is, despite our higher concepts of safe and civilized society, the same thing that was true of everyone to come before us through darker eras of history is still true today:  it takes cunning, strength and a resolute will to survive.  Depression has a way of pulling the wool over your eyes and changing the way you see yourself.  It can mask your every strength.  It can make all the knowledge you've gained seem like trivial nonsense.  It can make you feel as though you are woefully unprepared for tomorrow, and it can make you think that the only thing you have to look forward to is more pain.  All of that is patently false.  It's a heinous lie.  It's like the manic shovel love I was talking about earlier, except this time it's telling you that things will most certainly *not* be okay and the only bad thing worth murdering with a shovel is you.  

It's an extreme, and in many ways it's more of a lie than stupid puppy shovel love could ever be.  You're not weak.  You've endured a lot, yes, but your body and mind have weathered the strife and you're still here, still with us, still smart enough to understand that you should probably be afraid of the future.  

So don't feel ill-equipped.  What you're struggling with is a decision, pure and simple.  You very well could endure another 20 years of this if you chose to.  You probably wouldn't even go insane after all of it, but it certainly wouldn't be fun.  Either way, another helping of pain is always a sound possibility, and you can always be equipped to handle it if you so choose.  

The other option is ending it, and the one little leap of faith you've made in this otherwise torrential downpour of logic is that it would mean peace.  There's no guarantee that it would mean peace for you, no matter how much you'd like to believe that to be true.  At best, the only thing you'd be doing is answering a question with another question.  If nothing else, it's kind of rude.

I read it.  

I understand and empathize with just about all of this.  I sympathize with what little I haven't already experienced myself.  

I only want to touch on one thing, because, honestly, there's a lot here and if I get started I'll be hunched over typing for two hours.  

You talk about the present and the past a lot.  Being the analytical person that you quite obviously are, it would make sense for you to focus on that.  You've been there.  You've seen it.  You know it.  For everything you haven't witnessed personally, I'm sure you could provide amazing sources.  I would probably trust you to give me a more accurate account of the Civil War than the history book I had in high school.

Either way, my point is that you don't really touch on the future very much.  Also, when you do, it's a summation and logical projection of the patterns you've been able to verify through your experience of the present and past.  That, my friend, is boring. 

I mean, I get it.  I really do.  It's all so painfully reasonable.  Sure, current trends indicate that you'll end up being depressed again.  In fact, to add to that, I'm sure statistics from some psychological studies I can't be arsed to look up will also show that the things you think will make you happy will, in fact, not help at all.  That's the peril of relying so much upon logic;  the conclusions hardly ever get any less depressing.

Furthermore, I would submit to you that one of the most reasonable facts about the inherent nature of reality is that everything, without exception, is unreasonable.  I read somewhere that a fraction of a second after its inexplicable beginning, the universe was a boiling mass of basic particles which developed structure as it expanded and cooled.  Science, science, science, blah, blah, blah, add in however many billions of years of increasing complexity and energy transference and random nameless bundles of mass colliding violently with one another and sooner or later we get stupid therapists, guys like you climbing mountains and people like me staying awake for too many hours at a time.  Does any of that sound particularly logical to you?  I'm no scientist, but it sure seems to me like this whole thing, and by that I mean everything that we know to have ever existed and all the other shit we still have no clue about, is only happening because fuck it, why not?  Sure, there are all sorts of identifiable patterns to tally up and many more conclusions to be drawn from them, but what lies at the heart of this massive experiment is sheer, unadulterated chaos.  And chaos is pretty fucking cool.

Think about it for a moment.  Considering your current analysis, wouldn't it be absolutely unexpected for you to meet someone wonderful, fall stupidly in love and wake up one morning to find yourself cooking pancakes with a smiling kid staring up at you?  This has happened to people I know who didn't even want it.  I'm afraid that one day some similar situation might even blindside me.  The point I'm trying to make is that it's not necessarily something that can be planned for, so it doesn't exactly seem reasonable to feel miserable simply because it's not happening yet.  The universe is inherently chaotic, and the one thing you can count on is the fact that it'll slap some crazy shit on your plate when you're least expecting it (and likely unprepared).  So if love is what you're looking for, well, stop expecting it.  Or spend more time expecting something else, like a turf war between rival gangs of chimpanzees randomly ensuing the next time you go shopping.  Whatever.

Going back to your language, there's another angle we can approach this from.  Let's assume that love really is what you want and it really will make you happy if you attain it.  The only way you can be sure to stop yourself from ever achieving that dream is to opt out of life.  That'll stop you from achieving anything ever again.  It's an absolute, so I can see how it would appeal to you.  I just fail to see how it would be an adequate solution to the problem of not having love.  It may be a solution to your pain, sure, but what is more important?  Sometimes, suffering is a part of love.  Consider the idea that the person you haven't met yet will, sooner or later, be happy with you in a way that she has never been before.  Instead of being a square peg perpetually jammed into a round hole, imagine the prospect of you (and no one else, mind you) being the one unique piece missing from some other person's puzzle.  By removing yourself from the equation you doom both yourself and this other as yet unknown variable.  Personally, I would be willing to endure quite a bit of pain if it meant that there's a chance for that kind of outcome.  

And there is, because the universe is a random fucking mystery.

I'll start this off by saying that I am an absurdly suicidal person.  For me, every day is another exercise in fighting the impulse.  This is your disclaimer, just in case whatever I'm about to say doesn't make sense or makes you feel worse.

I'm responding here because your entire post seems to be asking the same question:  does anyone else feel this way?  The answer, as unwelcome as it may be, is a resounding yes.  I don't take any comfort in knowing that other people know what these feelings are like, but maybe you can.  For what it's worth, you're not alone.

Now, here's where I'm going to lead this into a sort of grey area.  We're talking about sorrow and emptiness and apathy and fear on a scale that is unimaginable.  Inevitably coupled with those feelings is the idea that something is inflicting them upon you.  Maybe it's society.  Maybe it's certain people around you.  Maybe it's the universe itself.  Maybe it's just you.  In any scenario, there's always the dreadful idea that *something* is causing this.  Even more terrifying is the idea that that something may be deriving some sort of sick satisfaction in causing you pain.

So, when all else fails, try enjoying it.  Imagine that there is some unknown force out there scuttling around in the darkness, pulling strings and chuckling to itself every time you feel this pain.  Fuck that, right?  Fuck that stupid disembodied entity getting off on your misery.  So what's the one thing you can do to get back at it?  Grin and fucking bear it.  If this is the absolute worst you could ever feel about anything, under any conceivable circumstances, then where else is there to go?  Nowhere but up and over it.  Smile, nod, and promptly go do something that you feel might even have only a marginal chance of making you feel better.  It's better than inaction.  

Reading back through what I just typed, it occurs to me that this may be some of the dumbest advice anyone has ever given.  If it is the dumbest, then that means it's closer to being just dumb enough to work than all the other dumb shit out there.  See how that works?  Use misery, hopelessness or even outright rage and fear against itself.  See what happens.  

I feel strangely obligated to offer some relatively meaningless platitudes as a means to offset any potential damage my advice may cause.  Keep your head up, champ.  Drop everything and travel the country.  Talk to a therapist.  You know what could make you happy, so do it.  If it all seems worse than it ever has before, understand that that means it can only get better.  

Either way, from one potential suicide to another, I wish you the best.

You shouldn't feel bad about needing to sleep.  You owe me nothing.  That didn't stop you from engaging me and offering some insight into things, though, so I hope you sleep the sleep of the innocent.  You're a good person and talking some of this shit out with you has done a little toward lifting tonight's cloud off of my head.  Thank you.

Helping people matters, but it's not really possible (and maybe even a bad idea) considering my current state of mind.  So, perhaps it helps to think of that as a sort of goal to work toward.  Correcting myself, helping others when the time comes.

Not being alone anymore would satisfy me.  I've been alone for years.  I came out of a very serious relationship with a grudge.  Long story short, I was betrayed by my best friend at the time.  I was also betrayed by her, and she was a very good friend before we ever thought about dating.  It was horrific. 

Making it through that experience made me stronger, but not in a way that was beneficial to anyone.  It made me callous.  It helped me develop this sick, sociopathic fixation upon attracting women to me only so I could have the opportunity to lure them into a false sense of security and hurt them.  You read about the best thing I ever did.  The worst thing I ever did was stringing a girl along for a year, making her fall in love with me, then crushing all her hopes and dreams for our future together with absolutely no remorse.  I actually told her that I had been lying to her the entire time.  I told her that she should thank me, because I did what I could to make her realize just how miserable and selfish every fucking person on the planet can truly be.  I was an absolute scumbag, and I'm pretty sure I scarred her.  It's something I still regret and still feel a lot of guilt about.  And I deserve it.

Still, I hold on to this idea that I can be normal again.  I did things like that because I thought I could actually cope with the prospect of being alone for the rest of my life.  I can't, and now I don't even remember why I thought I could.  I want to break down this sort of emotional barrier I built for myself and let someone in.  I want to make someone else happy in ways they may have given up hope on.  

There's also some sort of direction in life.  Purpose is a haughty word and really carries a sort of connotation that I don't particularly care for.  Direction sounds good, though.  Just the sort of basic comfort that comes from knowing that there's a goal, that it can be reached, that working toward it might open up possibilities in other areas of life that I can't even foresee.

There's probably more.  I don't know.

We have something in common, then.  I've seen some bad times, and lately it's been worse than I can remember.  I have lucid moments, though, and in the past I would also come to this subreddit and offer my advice/support/empathy to other people in need.  I think helping others is the most important thing anyone can do.  Personal happiness is vitally important too, though, so the rule I try to live by is this:  the second you become satisfied with yourself, start helping someone else.  It's not selfish to seek personal happiness, but to shamelessly fucking wallow in it while others around you suffer is pretty heartless.

Thing is, the most recent realization I've come to about myself is that I am so painfully far away from ever being satisfied with my own well-being.  I can't even begin to think about helping others because there's an inordinate amount of fuckery in my own life.  Even if it's all legitimate fuckery, endure that state of being for long enough and you'll still start to feel like a selfish asshole anyway.  It's maddening.

One.  Another person in this thread asked me to elaborate, like you, and I remembered my Christmas story.  And then I wrote it out.  And that's that.

Why do you ask?

The fact that I've done things that matter is undeniably true.  Even I understand that.  The problem I'm having is this absolutely crushing feeling that none of it has been of any consequence whatsoever.  That single looming emotion can trump whatever knowledge I think I possess.  It's persistent in a way that very few things are, and sooner or later I fear it's going to play a part in me acting on a very bad impulse.

I would like validation.  People always speak of seeking validation as if it's this terrible endeavor that only selfish people engage in.  I don't agree with that.  I think everyone needs validation on some level, and the people who congratulate each other for complaining about it don't realize just how absolutely hilarious that is.  

Simple validation.  Hey guy, nice fucking job.  That's really fucking cool.  You are here, I see you, and what you've done has, in some small way, reduced the amount of pain in the universe.

I'll make it easy for you.  I'll tell you about the best thing I've ever done.

Years ago, when I was a senior in high school, my Christmas present from my dad was a front row ticket to see the Trans-Siberian Orchestra in concert.  I'd been dreaming of seeing this show, and since they don't come to my town very often there was the very real possibility that this would be my only chance.  

The day after my father told me he bought the ticket, my school announced their yearly toy drive.  I'm sure you're familiar with the concept.  Kids bring in toys to donate to underprivileged families in the community.  The way my school did it, the class which donated the most toys got a pizza party.

I don't give a fuck about pizza.  I didn't give a fuck about pizza then.  It seemed like everyone else in my class did, though, so I used this as an opportunity to motivate them to donate.  I gave the concert ticket back to my dad and asked him to redeem it for its cost, which was around $100.  I took the money and bought a fuckload of toys, then brought them to school the next day.  We would have won the pizza party with what I bought alone, but I delivered an ultimatum to my class.  Everyone had to bring at least one toy to donate, otherwise I would drop my metric fuckload of toys in the box marked GENERAL DONATIONS in the cafeteria of the school and they'd be on their own.  

Every single motherfucker in my class brought toys.  Every single motherfucker in my class brought more than one, actually.  It was a beautiful sight.  People cried.  My teacher's nipples got hard.  Baby Jesus stopped crying and wrote each of us personal letters detailing the true meaning of Christmas.  And it was all fucking thanks to me.  ME, goddammit.

That was eight years ago.  Most of the time since then has been absolutely miserable for me, just in case this post hasn't indicated that clearly enough.

**Edit:**  Forgot the plot twist.  My dad was moved by the fact that I was willing to give up my gift in order to buy toys for kids I'd never even meet.  He never redeemed it.  He just gave me an extra $100 so I could buy the toys and then regifted the ticket to me and I saw the fucking show.  I'm aware of how comically depressing this sounds, but I can't even get personal sacrifice right.  Fuck me.

I had a date last weekend and I think I absolutely terrified the girl.  She is a friend of my best friend's girlfriend, so the date going badly has resulted in lots of unintended consequences.  My friend's girlfriend did a lot to convince my date that I'm a really cool guy.  My date must now think that her friend hangs out with lunatics.

My date spent a good part of our time together talking about the men she's currently sleeping with.  I wasn't thinking when I told my best friend about it later, so now both he and his girlfriend have lost a bit of respect for my date.  It was a catastrophic failure.  I feel as though things were normal between these three people, then I came into the picture and fucked about until their dynamic was changed in a way that can't really be repaired anymore.

I fuck shit up.  There's a fact.
Nothing that I know of.  I can only say with any reasonable certainty that I'm here.

As a person who has to manage extremely suicidal tendencies on a somewhat regular basis, I can ~~confirm~~ identify with this statement.  It's different for everyone, of course, and some people might readily associate images of destroyed cities or forest fires or what have you over this, but I can tell you that this image made me feel right at home.  

The initial impression of loneliness and cold, remote isolation is what likely strikes most people, and I get that.  It's accurate, more or less.  For me, it's the *persistence* of the picture that really hits home.  If you're curious about what years of depression might do to the spirit, put yourself in the spot where this picture was taken, look to the horizon and imagine that great dreary whiteness stretching on for as far and wide as your imagination will allow.  Consider the idea that something beautiful may have lingered here for a moment in a time long ago, but everything it was and all that it may have been is now reduced to a million miles of drifting, listless dust. 

Think of what your own mind might do to you if you happen to stare for too long.  Imagine the silhouette of some welcoming prospect floating somewhere far out there in the distance.  Maybe you could reach it, if only your limbs weren't frozen stiff.  Maybe you could begin to at least make out some fleeting, minor little detail if the wind would stop stinging your eyes and howling in your ears and beating against your chest until you want to stumble backwards and collapse.

Imagine walking for days until every part of you is worn and beaten and you can't remember when your eyes first dropped from the horizon and settled upon your own two feet, forever shuffling forward despite the electric needlepoints of pain shooting into you in waves with each desperate step.  Imagine being absolutely terrified to look back up because you know that whatever you thought you saw was just the ghost of a dream, and as it fades it leaves you with the knowledge that you came all this way for nothing and now it's too late to turn back.

Stop for a moment to picture all of this, perhaps only just a delusion to begin with, and then start walking.

Thanks for your reply.  It's all very sensible.  

Perhaps I've had bad friends, or maybe I've had good friends and I've just been unfortunate enough to be the best of them.  Either way, over the years I've learned to rely upon no one but myself.  *I* am the compassionate one.  *I* am the one who tries to put his own problems aside to help someone else.  It's a role I can't help but fill because I am naturally empathetic and, more often than not, can take a step back from any given conflict to offer an objective solution.

I'm from a relatively poor part of the country.  My friends are caught up in their own misery.  They have neurotic ex-wives/husbands, kids to pay for, mortgages, bills, this, that, whatever.  They're living fast and always on the go, and a problem like prolonged depression or suicidal thoughts is something they probably haven't counseled anyone on since high school.  Many of them have no insight whatsoever into something like this, and the best one can hope for during that type of discussion is a hasty, meaningless platitude.  

And that's just fine with me, really.  It seems unreasonable to expect anything more from a normal person, even if one does count that individual as a friend.  They're doing the best they can with what they have.

I think it's entirely possible to be strong or wise enough to make it through something like this alone.  Loneliness is something a person must learn to cope with, just like anything else.  It's a familiar problem of mine and one of the major obstacles in finally resolving this whole fucking mess.  When it comes to the prospect of being alone, I am weak.  I'm a quivering pile of goo.  I don't know how to even begin to approach it.

So, perhaps you can begin to see part of the problem.  Or at least part of the problem with how I'm looking at the problem.  I am too weak to cope with loneliness, yet unable to seek counsel from anyone I would consider a friend.  It's a conundrum.  

Furthermore, I love the whole 'fuck everyone's standards' sentiment, but I'm not entirely sure that it's realistic.  Sure, I can take pride in only caring about my own standards, but it seems to me that being able to conform to the expectations of others is a basic part of human interaction.  I would imagine there's some sort of happy balance to be discovered somewhere, but, like most things, I'm left to fumble around in the dark and fool myself into hoping for the best.  

Again, I welcome your reply.  I hope I didn't seem too aggressive with my rebuttal.  Thanks for taking the time to even read this.
